At the public library in my old neighborhood, there was a drawer marked MAPS THAT NO LONGER HELP. Nobody knew who had written the label. It was not an official category. The official categories were much less interesting. Inside lay a bus map from before the river bridge, a plan of a department store that had become apartments, and a walking guide to trees, several of which had evidently walked away. On rainy afternoons I would open the drawer and choose somewhere impossible to go. This was cheaper than traveling and, in certain respects, required a better pair of shoes.

One Saturday I selected the department store. Its directory promised notions, linens, a portrait studio, and a restaurant called the Copper Pear. I wanted especially to find notions. As a child I had imagined these were thoughts available for purchase, arranged by price and usefulness. A mild suspicion might cost a nickel. A conviction would come wrapped in brown paper. Even after I learned that notions meant buttons and thread, the word retained its original merchandise for me. I copied the floor plan onto the back of an envelope and set off in a drizzle fine enough to wear indoors.

The building stood on Alder Street. Its new entrance occupied the old display window, so that everyone arriving home briefly became something for sale. A man in green slippers was collecting his mail. I explained my errand, expecting embarrassment to end it. Instead he examined my envelope and said, “My kitchen is hosiery.” He sounded pleased. He introduced himself as Leon and offered to show me upstairs. We rode an elevator whose brass indicator still swept a little arc above the door, although the needle now pointed steadily between two and three, maintaining a private opinion about our actual altitude.

Leon's apartment smelled of toast. Hosiery had excellent light. Through a tall window I could see the wet roofs of buses pausing at the intersection and, farther off, a woman on a balcony squeezing rainwater from a yellow cushion. Leon set the envelope on his table. His late wife, he said, had worked in the portrait studio when they were young. She disliked photographing babies but had a gift for husbands. She asked them to calculate seventeen times six. In the instant after they found the answer, each wore a look of modest accomplishment that his family recognized as happiness.

Did he have a portrait she had taken? He did, but it was not of him. From a shelf he brought down a photograph of a pear on a white plate. The fruit had one leaf, withered at the edges, and a bruise shaped like Australia, assuming Australia had suffered some coastal erosion. His wife had taken it on her last afternoon at the store. The restaurant was already closed. Someone had left the pear by the register, perhaps as payment, perhaps because there are only so many objects a person can carry out of a life in one trip.

We drank tea. I asked whether he remembered where the notions counter had been. Without looking at my envelope he pointed directly down. “Mrs. Vale,” he said. “She does alterations. You'll appreciate that.” We found her door propped open with a dictionary, the heavy kind that used to settle disputes by the sheer sound of landing on a table. Inside, a boy stood on a stool while Mrs. Vale pinned his trousers. His socks displayed small, disreputable frogs. He was going to a wedding, he informed us, but was not himself getting married. He wished to make that distinction clear.

When he stepped down, Mrs. Vale considered the floor plan. She had indeed arranged her sewing machine almost exactly where the old notions counter had stood. This struck me as a marvelous coincidence until she explained that both positions were beside the only convenient electrical outlet. I liked the explanation better. A coincidence closes neatly, like a clasp. An outlet opens onto a whole history of practical decisions: someone needed light there, someone drilled through plaster, someone else, decades later, refused to spend good money on an extension cord. The boy practiced walking solemnly. His frogs rose and fell. 

By then the rain had stopped. I thanked them both and went outside, where sunlight shone on a puddle full of scaffolding. I still had an hour before the library closed. On the envelope I drew Leon's table, the elevator needle, the dictionary, and two frogs, one noticeably more competent than the other. Then I crossed the street to see the building from a distance. In a third-floor window a man in green slippers raised one hand. From below, the gesture looked like a shopkeeper turning a sign from CLOSED to OPEN, or possibly the other way around.

Back at the library, the woman at the desk supplied a fresh envelope because mine had developed a tea ring across the linens department. I decided to keep the ring. She watched me tuck my drawing behind the directory and asked whether I had found what I wanted. I said yes, although in fact I had not known what I wanted until a few minutes earlier. I had wanted the past to be somewhere other than behind me. Upstairs from a sewing machine seemed a perfectly satisfactory arrangement. The librarian shut the drawer gently with her hip.

Years later, when the library moved, I went to the sale of its old furniture. The map cabinet was gone. I bought a small oak stool instead, an awkward thing to carry home on a crowded bus. A little girl asked what it was for. I was about to say reaching high shelves, but she had already put her toy rabbit on it. The rabbit sat upright in the aisle, facing forward, the only passenger with a seat perfectly suited to its legs. We rode that way for six stops. When the girl got off, she thanked me for bringing the rabbit's chair.
